title: Holi: the festival of colors
hook: Prahlad walks out of the fire unharmed; the next morning everyone throws color and nobody is a stranger
tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diwali, the row of lamps on the darkest night. Your line was light the way home. Did you leave a light on for someone? Today, a fire the night before, and color the morning after. Day six hundred seventy-four.

In the days before Holi, in many villages and city lanes, a pile starts to grow at a crossroads or an open patch of ground: branches, scrap wood, cakes of dried cow dung, whatever people can spare. Sometimes a small figure is set on top. On the full-moon night, people gather around it at dusk. They walk around it, offer grain and coconut, and then they light it. Tomorrow these streets will be pink and green. Tonight belongs to the fire, and the fire has a name.
screen: `A PILE GROWS AT THE CROSSROADS.` → `LIT ON THE FULL-MOON NIGHT.` → `THE FIRE HAS A NAME.`

segments.voice: The bonfire is called Holika Dahan, the burning of Holika. The story behind it belongs to a demon king, Hiranyakashipu, who has made himself almost impossible to kill and demands to be worshiped. His own son, Prahlad, a boy, won't do it. Prahlad is devoted to Vishnu, and says so. The Bhagavata Purana tells how the king tried again and again to destroy his son, and how every attempt failed. The version Holi remembers adds the king's sister, Holika. In the story people tell, Holika could not be harmed by fire, and she sits in a blazing pyre with the boy in her lap, to burn him. Instead, the fire takes her, and Prahlad walks out unharmed, still saying the name of Vishnu. So the bonfire is a remembering: the cruelty burned, the trusting child safe. Then comes the morning. The day after the full moon of Phalguna, at the edge of spring, the streets fill with gulal, colored powder, and water. And for that one morning, the usual lines blur. Neighbors who don't speak, bosses and workers, old and young, all get the same handful of pink on the face. Nobody can tell who anyone is, and that's partly the point. Many people use Holi to visit, forgive, and start again. The story is about a boy who wouldn't bow to a tyrant. The festival turns it into a morning when nobody stands above anybody else.
screen: `HOLIKA DAHAN: THE BONFIRE.` · `PRAHLAD WON'T BOW.` · `THE FIRE TAKES HOLIKA, NOT THE BOY.` · `GULAL: THE SAME COLOR ON EVERYONE.` · then, large: `EVERYONE'S THE SAME COLOR TODAY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one small grudge, not the biggest one, just a small one you've been carrying: someone who didn't reply, a remark that stung. Picture it as a stick of wood. On an out-breath, lay it on a fire and watch it catch. You don't have to forgive the person yet. Just set down the stick, and feel your hands empty. The bell holds the time.
Holi. A bonfire for Prahlad's rescue from the fire, then a spring morning of color when everyone looks the same.
Your line: everyone's the same color today. Today, treat one person you'd normally rank above or below you as just exactly level with you. Day six hundred seventy-four.

screen: `DAY 674 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: MAHA SHIVARATRI: THE GREAT NIGHT OF SHIVA.`

howItsDone: On the full-moon night of Phalguna, many Hindus light the Holika Dahan bonfire and circle it with offerings; the next morning they play with colored powder and water, visit friends and family, and share sweets like gujiya.

myth: Holika Dahan means the burning of Holika
dahan is burning: the fire remembers the night Holika burned and Prahlad didn't.
in the story, the fire burns Prahlad and spares Holika
the fire takes Holika, and Prahlad walks out unharmed.
the colors are thrown on the full-moon night itself

fork.setup: you're Prahlad. your father, the king, demands that you worship him instead of Vishnu. what do you do?
options: keep your devotion and say so.
fork.reveal: he keeps his devotion openly, through every attempt on his life, and walks out of the fire unharmed.

original.note: Hindi and Sanskrit: holikā + dahana (burning). the bonfire on the night before the colors.

trapdoor: what you thought: Holi is a color party.
what it means: it's a bonfire for Prahlad's rescue, then a morning when every face wears the same color.
what a scholar hears: Holi falls on the full moon of Phalguna; the Bhagavata's seventh book tells Prahlad's story, while Holika's burning is the popular episode tied to the bonfire.
recall: touched with the tops of the grass

notes: Confirm that the Holika episode is not narrated in the Bhagavata Purana and identify its textual source if any (it appears in later Puranic and popular tradition).
Holika's protection from fire (a boon or a shawl) varies by telling; the script says only that fire could not harm her.
Holi date: the full moon of Phalguna (colors on the day after the bonfire in most of North India). Confirm.
